title: Dear Psychedelic Medicine: Congrats on Your AMA CPT Codes! Now, Get More Boring
subtitle: Starch that collar. This is Healthcare.
text:
Hi there, this is a column about my concerns with the progress of psychedelic medicine towards becoming just medicine.

The American Medical Association owns the current procedural terminology (CPT) code system (a trademark of the AMA). That is right, every time there is a bill submitted in healthcare, the intellectual property around the sequence of letters and numbers that describe that medical procedure? It is the is the property of the AMA. And this week, they announced that there would be experimental codes that described treatment with psychedelic medicine. This is important…ish1. This also means that the party is over. It is time for psychedelic treatments to get boring. Fast. It’s a cultural norm in the house of medicine.

American Medical Association (AMA) has approved a Current Procedural Terminology (CPT®) III code for psychedelic therapies. The full details of the code are expected to be released by the AMA in July 2023 and the code will go into effect when it is published on January 1, 2024.

Keep in mind, when I said fast before, it is in the context of a medical system so Byzantine that that press release just announces a decision was made. We will have some sense of what it means in July 2023. Eventually, we will know what the code is in 2024. This is lightning speed in the house of medicine. Buckle up! It is important to take your time to make sure the buckle goes in appropriately, and isn't in the wrong thing in the backseat, because it has to be the right buckle in the right plug for the buckle. You get the point. Buckling up is a process, not an event.

First, a disclosure. I have never used drugs recreationally in my life. And I think that particular piece of information is important to my point of view.

One of the powerful effects of psychedelic medicines is their ability to convince you they are powerful.

Their influence on selfhood and subject-object boundaries—known as ego dissolution—is surmised to underwrite their subjective and therapeutic effects. Agonism of 5-HT2A receptors, located at the apex of the cortical hierarchy, may have a powerful impact on sentience and consciousness. These effects can endure well after the pharmacological half-life, suggesting that psychedelics may affect neural plasticity, which may play a role in their therapeutic efficacy.

In short, anything that creates a powerful experience also creates powerful bias.

If you're trying to create a role for these compounds in the confines of the practice of medicine, it's essential to understand that culture. It is deeply conservative and scarred by its long history of scams. The institution of medicine is distrustful of broad claims. We are further distrustful of dirty hippies, thanks to the casual attitude of the 1960s enthusiasts. They underestimated what a deeply conservative medical establishment would think. I am speaking, of course, of Timothy Leary.

To quote the New Yorker on the topic of Dr. Leary:

The only things Leary was serious about were pleasure and renown. He underwent no fundamental transformation when he left the academic world for the counterculture. He liked women, he liked being the center of attention, and he liked to get high. He simply changed the means of intoxication. Like many people in those days, he started out on Burgundy but soon hit the harder stuff.

And skipping the bits about his troubled sex life life:

After his experience with Mexican mushrooms, Leary read “The Doors of Perception” with excitement. This was a style of mystico-pseudoscience that suited him perfectly, a kind of shamanistic psychology delightfully immune to empirical challenges.

This one man's personal ambition and entitlement led to statements that doomed psychedelic compounds cringe + criminality:

Yes Mr. Leary, yes. I actually agree with you. And you need to take that risk seriously….alas:

He was content to build his personal brand by making provocative statements that insured he would be famous but psychedelics would not be medicine. Further:

I get it. Your special. You're a snowflake. But that doesn't get some thing to be paid for by United healthcare in this day and age. That is the history we have to reckon with.

The controlled substances act put an end to the legal good times, and today serious science of Sandoz pharmaceuticals and others. And we lived without these powerful treatment options till right now still, for most.

I want to point out I don't want this to happen again. I spend an hour every day trying to get legally controlled substances to a pharmacy with them in stock. The DEA is no joke. Unfortunately, medical culture is really into somber stuff. And that means the following email from MAPS— literally today— is a terrible idea if we are trying to build legitimacy in traditional medical circles.

Now, there's nothing wrong with having a festival-like atmosphere at a festival. But I'm going to compare this to an announcement from a medical education sponsored by a traditional medical society: ( a note: I'm just pulling all these from my actual inbox to avoid the risk of cherry-picking)

And the American psychiatric association is like a goddamn rave compared to most of medicine; here is the first email that I found in my inbox from the New England Journal of Medicine about psychiatry:

Share The Frontier Psychiatrists

I hope you're noticing a theme. It is boring. It is not a festival-like atmosphere. Festival-like atmospheres make us think about many things. Unfortunately, “Revolutionary Science” is not one of the things we will think about.

I believe psychedelic medicine has tremendous promise. I think the people who brought science to this point are brave outsiders. But most of them, let's be honest, have done drugs. Those humans were cool once—or might still be. The audience they need to convince, however, includes deeply uncool people. I have never done drugs. Not just because I am scared. It is because, during formative years, I might never have been invited to that kind of party.

Tone down the fun. Turn up the boring. Trust me. I'm a doctor.

—Owen Scott Muir, M.D.

1These codes are experimental in nature, and have no relative value units assigned to them, which means there's no way to convert them into how much anybody would get paid. This is a level of detail that I'm not gonna get into, but I have it on good authority that experts in the space will be doing so promptly. After, of course, the appropriate review of rules and regulations as they relate to the conversion of relative value units… OK I just fell asleep too!
